title: Google's early attempt to pay websites for AI answers is struggling
gist: Google's pilot paying roughly 100 publishers when their content contributes to AI search answers is producing payouts that, for many small and mid-sized sites, equal about 0.1% of ad revenue, prompting larger publishers to refuse to join. Lawsuits from the NYT and Penske Media, a UK opt-out order and an EU antitrust probe add pressure on Google's AI search model.

insights.claim: Google has admitted about 100 publishers to an AI contribution pilot that pays websites when their content materially contributes to Gemini-powered search results such as AI Overviews.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Marks Google's first step away from its long-held refusal to pay publishers directly, a potential new cost line for Search.

insights.claim: Several small and mid-sized publishers in Google's AI pilot report payments equal to roughly one-tenth of one percent of their advertising revenue.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Payouts this small do not offset traffic losses, keeping publisher economics under pressure from AI search.
insights.quote: Google’s AI payments are miniscule, equaling roughly one-tenth of one percent of their advertising revenue
insights.locator: So far, publishers aren’t getting much

insights.claim: Several larger publishers have reportedly declined to join Google's AI payment pilot, hoping that holding out will force Google to offer a more generous deal.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Collective holdouts could raise Google's eventual content-licensing costs.
insights.locator: So far, publishers aren’t getting much

insights.claim: Payouts under Google's AI pilot vary widely: one early publisher is on track for over $1 million per year, a later entrant earned $50,000 to $60,000, and various smaller sites earned under $1,000 over several months.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Highly skewed payouts suggest the program favors a few winners rather than broadly sustaining the web ecosystem.
insights.locator: Payments under the program vary widely

insights.claim: Publishers in Google's AI pilot say niche topics with strong interest such as anime and gaming earn more, but it is unclear what counts as a meaningful contribution, making earnings impossible to plan.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Opaque, unpredictable revenue makes the pilot a weak basis for publisher business models.
insights.quote: It’s not clear what counts as a meaningful contribution to an AI answer, so it’s impossible to plan for future earnings.
insights.locator: In general, publishers in the test

themes.theme: Structural dependence of AI search on the open web

insights.claim: Google's traditional bargain of traffic in exchange for scraping is breaking down in the AI era, which is why the company launched the payment pilot.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: The web's traffic-for-content economic model is unravelling, threatening ad-supported publishers.
insights.quote: In the age of AI, that relationship is breaking down, hence the AI pilot.
insights.locator: Google has long resisted the idea

insights.claim: AI search answers often need backing from live web content, so if websites stop publishing or start blocking Google, AI search quality will decline.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Google's AI search moat depends on a healthy publisher ecosystem it is currently starving.
insights.quote: If websites stop publishing or start blocking Google, AI search quality will decline.

insights.claim: Small payments and the unclear nature of AI contributions could make expanding Google's pilot difficult, while ill will among publishers grows.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Scaling a fair compensation model may require much larger payouts than Google currently offers.
insights.quote: In the meantime, ill will is growing.
insights.locator: The AI contribution pilot is a step

insights.claim: The New York Times is suing Google for copyright infringement over AI training, and Penske Media (Variety, Rolling Stone) has sued Google over lost traffic, arguing that tying AI scraping to web indexing is unfair.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Litigation risk could force structural changes to how Google uses publisher content in AI.
insights.locator: Some publishers have already started fighting back

insights.claim: The UK government ordered Google to give publishers an AI opt-out that does not penalize them in organic search, and the European Commission is running an antitrust probe into whether Google fairly compensates publishers for AI answers.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Regulatory action could decouple AI scraping from search indexing and impose compensation obligations.
insights.locator: Regulators are starting to take notice

insights.claim: Given Google's recent track record in the EU, the European Commission's probe into AI-answer compensation seems unlikely to go in Google's favor.
insights.speaker: Ryan Whitwam
insights.so_what: Investors should price in potential EU fines or mandated payments tied to AI search.
insights.quote: Given the company’s recent track record in the EU, it seems unlikely that will work out in Google’s favor.
insights.locator: Regulators are starting to take notice
